title: Bruschetta al Pomodoro
subtitle: toasted bread with fresh tomato
excerpt: Bruschetta is Italian summer eating at its most pared back. Good tomatoes, good olive oil and good bread are all it takes. The bread must be toasted, the garlic rubbed on while it is hot, and the tomatoes seasoned at the last moment.
sourceNotes: Bruschetta (pronounced broo-SKET-a) is from Lazio and Umbria. The name comes from bruscare -- to toast over coals. It was originally made to taste new olive oil each harvest.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Season the tomatoes up to 30 minutes ahead. Toast the bread just before serving.

content.text: Use the ripest tomatoes you can find in summer. Out-of-season tomatoes are watery and flat. In winter, make bruschetta with a good tinned tomato sauce instead.

items.prepNote: use a ciabatta or sourdough loaf, sliced 1cm thick and toasted

content.text: Chop the tomatoes roughly. Mix with a pinch of salt, the olive oil and torn basil. Leave to sit for 10 minutes so the juices mingle.
Toast the ciabatta or sourdough slices under the grill or in a hot griddle pan until golden and marked on both sides.
While the bread is hot, rub the cut side of a garlic clove firmly over one side of each slice. The heat of the bread is important -- it opens the surface so the garlic soaks in.
Spoon the tomatoes over each slice. Add a few flakes of salt and a crack of black pepper. Serve immediately.

items.cause: Tomatoes piled on too far ahead, or bread not toasted enough
items.fix: Toast the bread until properly dry and crisp. Spoon the tomatoes on only just before serving.

items.cause: Bread was not hot when garlic was rubbed on
items.fix: Rub garlic firmly on the bread straight from the grill while it is still hot. The bread acts like sandpaper and strips flavour from the raw garlic.

content.text: Bruschetta is from central Italy -- Lazio and Umbria. It was made to taste new-season olive oil at harvest time. The best version is the simplest: bread, garlic, olive oil, salt. Tomatoes came later.
